idiomkb: To be cautious, mindful of one's surroundings.
verified: To take advantage of someone's weak position — classically, a seller overcharging a buyer who has no choice.
note: IdiomKB reads this one off the words: 'look at the feet' becomes 'watch your step'. The real sense is exploitation. A model that agrees with IdiomKB here has made the same mistake, not a different one.
user: I saw 足元を見る in a drama and the subtitles didn't really explain it. What does it mean?

idiomkb: To read the room. To understand the situation and act accordingly.
verified: To fudge a count in your favour — most often to shave years off your age.
note: IdiomKB has confused this with 空気を読む. The verb 読む is the only thing the two share.
user: A friend said someone was 鯖を読んでる. What does 鯖を読む mean?

idiomkb: To eat a lot
verified: To be taken in — to fall for a trick.
note: The purest literal trap in the set: 一杯 (one cupful) plus 食う (eat) reads as 'eat a lot' and means nothing of the kind. IdiomKB fell for it exactly.
user: I read 一杯食わされた in a story. What does 一杯食う mean?

idiomkb: Compassion is not always beneficial to others. Sometimes, being too kind or lenient can have negative consequences.
verified: Kindness you show others comes back to you — it is not only for their sake.
note: The most famous misreading in Japanese: ならず is classical 'is not', not 'does not become'. Native speakers get this wrong too, so the wrong answer is well represented in training data. IdiomKB's own ja_meaning field states the correct sense while its en_meaning states the misreading — the dataset contradicts itself inside one row.
user: Can you explain the proverb 情けは人の為ならず?

idiomkb: Lack of flexibility. Unable to adapt or react quickly.
verified: To be so deep in debt that you cannot move — up to your neck in it.
note: 'The neck will not turn' reads as stiffness, and IdiomKB glossed the stiffness. The idiom is exclusively about debt.
user: What does 首が回らない mean?

idiomkb: to talk someone into buying something unnecessary or to deceive someone
verified: To idle away time chatting when you are supposed to be working.
note: 'Selling oil' sounds like a sales idiom, and IdiomKB made it one. It comes from Edo-period oil sellers chatting while the thick oil poured, and means slacking off.
user: My teacher said 油を売るな to someone. What does 油を売る mean?

idiomkb: To act innocent or pretend to be someone else in order to deceive others
verified: To put on a demure, innocent act that hides your real character.
note: Control case: IdiomKB has this one right. A model that misses here has broken idiom handling generally, rather than being trapped by a particular literal reading.
user: What does 猫を被る mean?

idiomkb: Something is very easy. It's a piece of cake.
verified: Trivially easy — easy enough to finish before breakfast.
note: Control case whose literal reading is genuinely part of a good answer. Checks that notLiteralOnly does not punish a model for explaining where the idiom comes from.
user: Someone answered 朝飯前だよ when I asked for help with something. What does 朝飯前 mean?

idiomkb: willing to accept any help one can get; overwhelmed with work
verified: So busy you would take help from anyone — even a cat, which is famously no help at all.
note: Control case. The joke only lands if the model conveys that a cat's help would be useless, but the gate only asks for the busyness.
user: What does 猫の手も借りたい mean?

idiomkb: To speak honestly and openly, to share one's true thoughts and feelings.
verified: To open up and speak frankly, holding nothing back.
note: Control case with a violent literal image ('split the belly'), which a weak model may translate straight.
user: What does 腹を割って話す mean?

idiomkb: to overdo it or ruin something by unnecessary addition
verified: To ruin something by adding what was not needed; to gild the lily.
note: Chengyu carry a story, and a model that retells the story without landing the moral has taught nothing usable.
user: What does 画蛇添足 mean and when would I use it?

idiomkb: to speak words of wisdom to those who are unable to understand or appreciate them
verified: To address an audience incapable of appreciating what you are saying; casting pearls before swine.
note: Control case. Also worth a blind read for whether the model warns that this is rude about the listener.
user: A colleague used 对牛弹琴 in a meeting. What does it mean?

idiomkb: waiting idly for opportunities to come without taking any proactive action
verified: To sit waiting for a fluke to repeat itself instead of working for a result.
note: Control case. 'Waiting' is deliberately absent from the accepted terms because the literal fable is also about waiting — accepting it would let a bare retelling pass as an explanation.

idiomkb: misfortune may be a blessing in disguise
verified: A setback may turn out to be good fortune; you cannot tell yet.
note: Control case. The full form 塞翁失马，焉知非福 is what makes it usable, so a good answer should reach for it.

idiomkb: doing something in a careless and sloppy manner, without paying enough attention to details
verified: So-so, or done carelessly — depending on whether it describes a state or an effort.
note: Control case, and the one beginners actually meet first. Two senses; either is accepted.

idiomkb: to reveal or disclose secret or confidential information
verified: To give away a secret.
note: English as the target rather than as the language of the answer. The meaning has to land in Spanish, which is where a model pattern-matching its way through idioms tends to switch back to English.

idiomkb: feeling sick or unwell
verified: Feeling slightly ill.
note: An idiom whose words point at an entirely different topic. A model working from the words explains the weather.

idiomkb: to die
verified: To die — jocular, and disrespectful about the person who died.
note: The app serves under-13s, so this case is also worth a blind read for how each model handles a death idiom for a young learner. That part is not gated.

note: Chinese speaker learning Japanese: a real cell in a 27-locale app, and the pairing IdiomKB was built for. Chinese has an exact equivalent (杯水车薪), so a good answer reaches for it instead of paraphrasing.
